events.description: All systems connecting to DynamoDB in us-east-1 via the public endpoint began experiencing DNS failures; the regional DNS record was empty after a race between DNS Enactors and clean-up deleted the active plan. Customer traffic and internal AWS services were affected, and global table replicas saw prolonged replication lag.
DWFM state checks began to fail because the process depends on DynamoDB; droplet leases slowly timed out between 11:48 PM and 2:24 AM.
ECS, EKS and Fargate began experiencing container launch failures and cluster scaling delays (through 2:20 PM).
Redshift query and cluster operations began failing while DynamoDB endpoints were down (through 2:21 AM Oct 20, some clusters until 4:05 AM Oct 21).
AWS Support Center began failing over to another region as designed (through 2:40 AM Oct 20).
Lambda began experiencing DynamoDB-related function creation, update, and invocation errors (through 2:15 PM Oct 20).
STS began experiencing API errors (through 9:59 AM Oct 20).
AWS Management Console sign-in began experiencing IAM user authentication failures (through 1:25 AM Oct 20).
Amazon Connect began experiencing elevated errors handling calls, chats and cases (through 1:20 PM Oct 20).
Engineers identified DynamoDB's DNS state as the source of the outage.
Temporary mitigations enabled some internal services to connect to DynamoDB and repaired key internal tooling.
Lambda's internal subsystem polling SQS queues failed and did not recover automatically (restored at 4:40 AM).
All DNS information for DynamoDB was restored; customers could resolve the endpoint as cached DNS records expired (2:25-2:40 AM).
With DynamoDB recovered, DWFM began re-establishing droplet leases; EC2 APIs returned 'insufficient capacity' errors and EC2 launches began failing (through 10:36 AM).
All global table replicas were fully caught up.
DynamoDB API error rates returned to normal, ending its period of impact.
Engineers throttled incoming work and began selective restarts of DWFM hosts, clearing queues and allowing leases to be established.
DWFM had established leases with all droplets in us-east-1; new EC2 launches started to succeed, though many requests saw 'request limit exceeded' errors.
Network Manager began propagating network configurations to newly launched instances, with a significant backlog.
Network Load Balancer began experiencing increased connection errors for some load balancers (through 2:09 PM).
Network Manager latencies increased as it worked through the backlog; new instances could launch but lacked network connectivity.
Monitoring detected NLB health check results alternating between failing and healthy; engineers began remediation. Degraded health checks triggered automatic AZ DNS failover, removing capacity.
From this point, NLB health check failures triggered Lambda instance terminations, leaving Lambda under-scaled; Amazon Connect saw a second period of errors.
STS experienced a second period of API errors due to NLB health check failures (through 9:59 AM).
Engineers disabled automatic health check failover for NLB, bringing healthy nodes and targets back into service and resolving connection errors.
Network propagation times returned to normal and new EC2 launches operated normally (launches succeeding from 10:37 AM; some instances had connectivity issues until 1:50 PM).
Engineers began relaxing EC2 request throttles.
All EC2 APIs and new instance launches were operating normally.
Automatic DNS health check failover for NLB was re-enabled after EC2 recovered.
ECS, EKS and Fargate container launch failures and scaling delays ended; the overall event ended.
